section_1.title: Prerequisite Review: The Two Pillars
section_1.content: Briefly recap derivatives as the 'slope of a tangent' (instantaneous change) and integrals as the 'area under a curve' (accumulation). Use a visualization of a moving car: speedometer (derivative) vs. odometer (integral).
section_1.example: A squirrel running: The speed graph shows how fast it moves at time 't', while the integral shows total distance covered.

section_2.title: The Conceptual Paradox
section_2.content: Pose the question: Why should the process of finding a slope be related to the process of finding an area? Introduce the 'Accumulation Function' F(x) = ∫[a to x] f(t)dt, representing the growing area under a curve.
section_2.example: Imagine a 2D printer head moving across a page; the 'area' fills up as the head moves, linking the rate of movement (f) to the accumulated ink (F).

section_3.title: The Fundamental Theorem (Part 1)
section_3.content: Visually demonstrate that the derivative of the accumulation function returns the original function: F'(x) = f(x). Use an animation where a rectangle's height changes as its width 'dx' expands, showing the instantaneous change in area equals the function height.
section_3.example: As a robotic arm traces a mountain silhouette, the rate at which the shaded area beneath it increases is exactly equal to the current height of the mountain at that specific point.

section_4.title: Practical Application: Calculating Net Change
section_4.content: Connect the theorem to evaluation: ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = F(b) - F(a). Explain that to find the area, we simply need the 'anti-derivative'—the inverse of a derivative.
section_4.example: Calculating the total weight gain of a bear over a season by integrating its daily weight-gain rate function from Spring to Autumn.

section_5.title: Summary: The Inverse Relationship
section_5.content: Synthesize the lesson: Differentiation and Integration are inverse operations, like addition and subtraction or multiplication and division. Reiterate that this relationship turns difficult infinite summations into simple algebraic evaluations.
section_5.example: Visual transition: A 'differentiation arrow' pointing one way and an 'integration arrow' pointing back, forming a closed logical loop.
